prompt: A state prosecutes a serious offense but denies a jury because its own constitution permits a bench trial. Which response is best?
options: The incorporated federal jury right sets a minimum the state must respect.
Only the state constitution matters.
Every petty offense must also have a jury.
The Fourth Amendment alone supplies the jury right.
explanation: Duncan applies the Sixth Amendment jury guarantee to serious state criminal prosecutions through the Fourteenth Amendment.

prompt: A state seeks a punitive forfeiture of a driver’s vehicle and argues that the federal Excessive Fines Clause restricts only federal officials. What is the best response?
options: The state is correct because forfeiture is always outside the Bill of Rights.
The clause also binds state and local governments; excessiveness must then be assessed on the facts.
Every forfeiture is automatically excessive.
The federal clause applies only if the owner was acquitted.
explanation: Timbs decided incorporation and remanded; applying the excessiveness standard to particular property is a separate step.

prompt: A capital defendant meets appointed counsel only as a rushed trial begins. What is the strongest constitutional inquiry?
options: Whether any lawyer’s name appeared in the file, ending the inquiry.
Whether the defendant can prove innocence before requesting preparation time.
Whether the defendant received a meaningful opportunity for counsel’s assistance.
Whether the appointment alone substitutes for all actual assistance.
explanation: Powell looked beyond nominal appointment to effective opportunity for assistance under its serious circumstances.

prompt: Police have probable cause to arrest a suspect. At trial, the prosecutor argues that this same showing is enough to convict. What is wrong?
options: An arrest conclusively proves the offense.
Reasonable suspicion suffices whenever the officer is credible.
A fair probability is the trial burden for every element.
Conviction requires proof of each offense element beyond a reasonable doubt, a higher burden.
explanation: Procedural stages serve different purposes and demand different levels of proof.

prompt: A new constitutional criminal-procedure rule is announced while a defendant’s ordinary direct appeal remains pending. What generally happens?
options: The new rule generally applies because the conviction is not yet final.
Only arrests made after the decision benefit.
The rule applies only if it changes which conduct is criminal.
Every pending appeal is treated as a final collateral case.
explanation: Griffith applies new rules to cases on direct review or not yet final.

prompt: A defendant’s state conviction was already final before the new jury-unanimity rule. He seeks that rule’s benefit on federal habeas review. What is the best analysis?
options: Every significant jury rule automatically reopens every final conviction.
The new procedural unanimity rule does not apply retroactively in that federal collateral proceeding.
The rule necessarily is substantive because jury trials are important.
Direct-review retroactivity automatically controls federal habeas.
explanation: Edwards treats Ramos as a new procedural rule and rejects retroactivity on federal collateral review.

prompt: A prisoner argues that a newly announced procedural right must reopen her final conviction on federal habeas because it is exceptionally important. Which response is best?
options: Any important procedural rule automatically qualifies for a watershed exception.
A new rule is substantive whenever a defendant strongly values it.
There is no continuing watershed-procedural-rule exception; importance alone does not supply retroactivity.
Finality never affects federal habeas analysis.
explanation: Edwards eliminated the proposed watershed-procedural-rule exception. Do not use the old Teague formulation without that update.

prompt: Two defendants invoke the same new rule. One is on ordinary direct appeal; the other is challenging a final conviction on federal habeas. Why can their results differ?
options: Only the defendants’ preferences matter.
Every rule applies identically in every proceeding.
The side with the older lawyer receives the new rule.
Finality and review posture determine different retroactivity frameworks.
explanation: Posture and finality identify the governing framework; then classify the rule and examine the relevant exceptions.

prompt: An officer physically installs a tracker on a suspect’s car to obtain information. Which analysis is necessary?
options: A physical intrusion on a protected effect to obtain information can itself be a search.
Public-road travel automatically excuses the physical installation.
No search is possible without property damage.
Only the owner’s subjective desire to hide the license plate matters.
explanation: An information-gathering physical intrusion on a protected effect can itself be a search.

prompt: Police electronically listen to a private call from outside a booth without physically entering it. Which proposition answers “no trespass, no search”?
options: A public location eliminates all privacy in conversations.
A reasonable expectation of privacy can be invaded without a physical trespass.
Only homes can be protected against listening.
A microphone outside the booth can never conduct a search.
explanation: The absence of a physical entry does not end the search inquiry.

prompt: An investigator both physically intrudes on a person’s protected property to obtain information and uses a method implicating reasonable privacy expectations. How should you analyze whether there was a search?
options: Require both routes to be satisfied in every case.
Ignore property whenever privacy is disputed.
Consider the property and privacy routes; either can independently establish a search.
Ignore privacy whenever there is no lasting physical damage.
explanation: Jones retained the reasonable-expectation framework and recognized an independent property-based ground.

prompt: After finding that government conduct was a search, what is the next useful inquiry?
options: Automatically dismiss all charges.
Automatically conclude the search was lawful.
Ignore the search’s scope.
Whether a valid warrant or a recognized justification made it reasonable.
explanation: “Search” triggers constitutional analysis; it does not decide reasonableness or the suppression remedy by itself.

prompt: Officers enter private farmland far beyond the home’s curtilage. The owner points only to no-trespassing signs. Do the signs alone establish a protected federal Fourth Amendment interest in the open field?
options: No; signs and private ownership alone do not defeat the open-fields doctrine.
Yes; every private acre is constitutionally a house.
Yes; a sign automatically creates curtilage regardless of location and use.
No; private ownership never matters anywhere, even inside the home.
explanation: Ownership, fences, and signs do not automatically create a Fourth Amendment privacy expectation in open fields.

prompt: A shed is near a home, inside its domestic fence, used for household activities, and screened from the road. Which analysis best addresses curtilage?
options: Count only the number of feet from the house.
Evaluate proximity, enclosure, use, and shielding together.
Treat every outbuilding on privately owned land as curtilage.
Ignore domestic use because the shed has a separate roof.
explanation: Dunn also considers enclosure and efforts to shield observation; the factors guide an overall judgment.

prompt: Officers use technology not in general public use to obtain details of a home’s interior otherwise unavailable without entry. They rely only on the fact that they stood on a public street. Best analysis?
options: Standing in public automatically makes every sensing technique constitutional.
The government must physically damage the house before a search occurs.
The described technological observation is a search despite the public vantage.
Only details that officers consider intimate receive protection.
explanation: Kyllo protects home information against the described sense-enhancing technology.

prompt: An officer uses a novel aerial surveillance method and argues that compliance with aviation rules alone defeats any Fourth Amendment objection. Which response is best?
options: Every lawful flight permits any kind of home surveillance.
Every observation from the air is automatically a search.
A backyard fence conclusively prevents all aerial observation.
Aviation legality alone is insufficient; the vantage, public use, technology, and intrusion into domestic privacy matter.
explanation: Aerial-observation cases are fact-specific. Evaluate the public vantage and method instead of treating aviation compliance or a fence as conclusive.

prompt: A suspect voluntarily tells an informant about a plan; the informant transmits the conversation to police. Does the suspect’s misplaced trust alone establish a Fourth Amendment violation?
options: No; a cooperating participant may relay the conversation without the same privacy claim as an outsider intercepting it.
Yes; a conversational partner can never disclose what was said.
Yes; electronic transmission always receives different treatment from participant disclosure.
No; this means police may intercept every private conversation between noncooperating people.
explanation: White addresses the risk that a conversation partner will cooperate with government; it differs from an outsider intercepting a private call.

prompt: A tracker reveals that a container is inside a residence, information unavailable from public observation. Police rely on the rule for tracking a limited public-road trip. Best response?
options: All tracking signals are abandoned property.
Learning otherwise unavailable information about the home’s interior presents a distinct protected intrusion.
Anything once transported on a road loses all later privacy.
Public-road tracking doctrine authorizes every interior-home observation.
explanation: Separate public movement from information about the inside of a home.

prompt: The government obtains at least seven days of historical cell-site location records from a carrier without a warrant or exception. Is third-party possession enough to defeat a search claim?
options: Yes; all business records receive exactly the same constitutional treatment.
Yes; location history can never reveal private activity.
No; this extensive historical location acquisition is a search and generally requires a warrant.
No search can occur unless police enter the carrier’s premises.
explanation: Carpenter declined mechanical application of the third-party doctrine to comprehensive historical location data.

prompt: Investigators want to use real-time cell tracking. They argue that a decision concerning historical location records conclusively approves their method. Which analytical response is best?
options: Assume every form of cell tracking is categorically approved.
Assume every form of cell tracking is categorically forbidden.
Ignore whether the requested data is historical or real-time.
Identify the technology and relevant authority; a narrow historical-records holding does not decide every tracking method.
explanation: Carpenter expressly left several technologies and circumstances unresolved.

prompt: A lawful stop is supported by suspected fare evasion. Does that alone permit a weapons frisk?
options: No. The officer also needs a reasonable basis to suspect the person is armed and dangerous.
Yes; every stop authorizes a full pocket search.
Yes; every offense is treated as an armed robbery.
No frisk is ever possible without an arrest warrant.
explanation: Terry separates the basis for a stop from the additional safety basis and limited scope of a frisk.

prompt: A dog sniff adds several minutes after the traffic mission is complete, with no independent reasonable suspicion. What result?
options: Any delay under 30 minutes is automatically valid.
The added detention is not justified merely because the sniff is brief.
A limited sniff automatically validates every seizure supporting it.
Car ownership supplies independent reasonable suspicion.
explanation: A sniff may be limited in informational scope yet the added seizure can still be unlawful.

prompt: Officers bring a drug dog to the front porch to investigate the home. What is the strongest relevant rule?
options: Every visitor may conduct any investigation on the porch.
The limited information from a sniff automatically defeats all property-based analysis.
The specialized investigative intrusion into curtilage exceeds the ordinary license to approach and constitutes a search.
A porch is always an open field.
explanation: The ordinary implied license to approach a door does not include a specialized detection investigation.

prompt: Police detain luggage for roughly 90 minutes to arrange a dog sniff. They argue the sniff reveals only contraband. Which objection remains?
options: The informational scope of the sniff automatically cures any detention.
Police always receive an automatic 90-minute allowance.
Luggage can never be detained under any circumstances.
The prolonged luggage seizure can be unreasonable even if the sniff itself is not a search.
explanation: Place rejected the extended detention rather than treating a contraband-only sniff as a cure for seizure problems.

prompt: An anonymous tip accurately predicts unusual future travel, which officers corroborate. How should probable cause be evaluated?
options: Consider the totality, including corroboration, basis of knowledge, and reliability.
Reject every anonymous tip automatically.
Require proof beyond a reasonable doubt before requesting a warrant.
Use only the informant’s name and ignore predictive detail.
explanation: Gates replaced rigid independent informant prongs with a practical totality inquiry.

prompt: An officer observes a real traffic violation but also hopes to investigate drugs. Which statement is correct?
options: An unspoken additional motive always invalidates the stop.
The additional motive generally does not invalidate an objectively justified traffic stop under the Fourth Amendment.
An objectively justified stop eliminates every possible Equal Protection claim.
Drug curiosity alone justifies a stop without objective facts.
explanation: Objective Fourth Amendment justification and an Equal Protection challenge are different questions.

prompt: Police have a warrant for a tavern and its bartender. They search an uninvolved patron solely because he is present. What is the strongest objection?
options: Every patron joins a criminal enterprise by entering the tavern.
A premises warrant authorizes all searches of all people present.
The search needs individualized justification; mere presence does not automatically supply it.
Only a patron who objects aloud retains Fourth Amendment rights.
explanation: Probable cause must be particularized; context explains the different outcomes.

prompt: An officer stops a car based on a mistaken interpretation of an ambiguous traffic law. Which question controls whether the legal mistake can support reasonable suspicion?
options: Whether the officer sincerely believed it, regardless of clarity.
Whether contraband was later found, retroactively validating the stop.
Whether the officer has ever made a traffic stop before.
Whether the mistake was objectively reasonable.
explanation: Heien permits a limited class of objectively reasonable mistakes of law.

prompt: A warrant’s application lists items, but the warrant itself omits them and does not incorporate the application. What is the concern?
options: The warrant lacks the required particularity; an unincorporated application does not cure that defect.
Probable cause replaces every description requirement.
The officer’s memory supplies any missing warrant terms.
The application always becomes part of the warrant automatically.
explanation: The operative warrant must meet particularity; unincorporated supporting papers do not cure the omission.

prompt: Evidence is probably stored at a third party’s office, but the owner is innocent. Does that alone prohibit a warrant?
options: Yes; every premises owner must first be charged with a crime.
No; a sufficient evidence-place connection can support a warrant, subject to applicable safeguards.
Yes; warrants may never reach third-party evidence.
No protections apply because the owner is innocent.
explanation: An innocent owner is not a categorical Fourth Amendment bar; press materials can receive additional statutory protection.

prompt: A defendant substantially shows that an officer knowingly inserted a false statement essential to the warrant’s probable cause. What should the court consider?
options: Refusing any inquiry because a warrant can never be challenged.
Automatically acquitting without identifying the evidence.
A hearing on the affidavit’s material falsity; if proved and the remaining affidavit is insufficient, suppression may follow.
Treating deliberate falsity as protected whenever the officer hoped to solve a crime.
explanation: Franks provides a path to challenge deliberate or reckless falsehood material to probable cause.

prompt: An officer knowingly included a false statement in a warrant affidavit, but the remaining truthful facts independently establish probable cause. Why does that matter to suppression based on affidavit falsity?
options: It makes the deliberate lie acceptable professional conduct.
It automatically validates every separate search in the investigation.
It eliminates the need for a neutral issuing official.
The falsehood’s materiality to probable cause is required for that suppression theory.
explanation: The Franks suppression inquiry asks whether the warrant depends on the deliberate or reckless falsehood.

prompt: Officers executing a valid contraband warrant briefly detain an occupant at the searched home to secure the operation. Is a separate arrest justification invariably required?
options: No; limited occupant detention incident to that search can be reasonable, subject to its limits.
Yes; every brief detention is a full custodial arrest.
No; the warrant authorizes detention anywhere for any duration.
No; every occupant is automatically guilty of the suspected crime.
explanation: Summers recognizes limited detention authority tied to executing the premises search.

prompt: Police invoke a blanket policy of never knocking in drug cases. What is the problem?
options: All drug searches automatically qualify for no-knock entry.
Dispensing with announcement requires case-specific reasonable suspicion of danger, futility, or interference such as evidence destruction.
No-knock entry is forbidden even in genuine danger.
Announcement has no connection to Fourth Amendment reasonableness.
explanation: Wilson recognizes the principle; Richards rejects a categorical felony-drug exception. Banks also makes timing contextual.

prompt: Officers reasonably think a floor is one apartment but discover two during the search. What should they do?
options: Continue throughout both because the initial mistake was reasonable.
Treat both occupants as automatically guilty.
Limit the search once the mistake becomes apparent.
Destroy the warrant and deny that any search occurred.
explanation: Garrison evaluates both initial reasonableness and execution as new facts emerge.

prompt: Officers use handcuffs on occupants during a dangerous weapons search, then keep everyone restrained long after the safety need and search end. What is the best analysis?
options: A warrant validates all later restraint indefinitely.
Every use of handcuffs during a search is unconstitutional.
A dangerous search suspends all limits on treatment of occupants.
Assess the restraints’ reasonableness as circumstances and duration change; an initial safety basis is not unlimited authority.
explanation: Muehler and Rettele uphold particular safety measures on particular facts, not unlimited force.

prompt: Police follow a fleeing suspected misdemeanant into a home. They identify flight but no further emergency facts. Which analysis is required?
options: Evaluate actual exigency under all the circumstances; misdemeanor flight does not create an automatic entry exception.
Every misdemeanor pursuit automatically permits home entry.
No misdemeanor can ever create any emergency.
A pursuing officer’s preference to enter settles reasonableness.
explanation: Lange rejects both an automatic pursuit exception and a rule ignoring genuinely urgent circumstances.

prompt: Officers invoke general community caretaking to enter a home and seize firearms, without identifying consent, a warrant, or an actual emergency. What is missing?
options: Nothing; all firearms eliminate home protection.
A recognized justification for the home intrusion; vehicle caretaking alone does not supply one.
Only proof that the officers acted politely.
Nothing; welfare-related purposes automatically authorize all home searches.
explanation: Analyze emergency aid or another actual exception separately from general community caretaking.

prompt: Officers lawfully knock and then hear evidence apparently being destroyed. Does the knock alone improperly create the exigency?
options: Yes; officers may never lawfully knock on a door.
No; an unlawful threatened entry always creates a valid exception.
No, if the officers did not create it through conduct violating or threatening to violate the Fourth Amendment.
Yes; an evidence emergency can never follow an officer’s lawful approach.
explanation: Lawful investigation can prompt a reaction without disqualifying the exception; an actual exigency must still exist.

prompt: Police immediately pursue an armed robber into a house. What limits the resulting search?
options: Nothing; they may search for any unrelated evidence indefinitely.
Only the owner’s choice of paint color.
They must ignore all immediate danger until a trial begins.
The urgent need to find the suspect, weapons, and address the emergency.
explanation: Hayden permits action responsive to urgency; scope remains tied to justification.

prompt: A routine DUI investigation leaves practical time to obtain a warrant, but an officer draws blood without consent based solely on natural alcohol dissipation. Best analysis?
options: Dissipation alone is not a categorical exigency; evaluate the actual circumstances and warrant practicality.
Every DUI automatically authorizes a warrantless blood draw.
Dissipation may never be considered, even in a genuine emergency.
All biological samples fall outside the Fourth Amendment.
explanation: Dissipation is a factor, not a universal substitute for analyzing practical circumstances.

prompt: After a lawful DUI arrest, police request a breath test and a needle blood draw, relying solely on search incident to arrest. Which distinction matters?
options: Both tests always fit the exception in exactly the same way.
The breath test generally fits that exception; the blood draw generally needs a warrant or a separate justification.
Neither test can ever proceed without a warrant.
The more intrusive test automatically gets fewer protections.
explanation: Birchfield distinguishes breath from the more intrusive blood test.

prompt: A suspected drunk driver becomes unconscious and is taken to a hospital while officers face urgent medical and investigative demands. Which is the most careful approach to a warrantless blood draw?
options: Unconsciousness conclusively authorizes every bodily search.
The driver’s inability to object is voluntary consent.
Analyze the unconscious-driver exigency framework and its qualifications, including whether unusual facts made a warrant practical.
Hospital admission automatically eliminates all Fourth Amendment rights.
explanation: The opinion was fractured and its factual qualifications matter.

prompt: A state criminally punishes refusal of a warrantless blood test justified only by legally implied consent to drive. What is the central problem?
options: Driving automatically waives every bodily privacy interest.
A state may impose any penalty to manufacture consent.
Blood and breath tests always receive identical search-incident treatment.
Criminal refusal penalties cannot by themselves justify the otherwise unauthorized blood search.
explanation: Birchfield distinguishes criminal punishment for refusing an otherwise unauthorized blood test from civil licensing and evidentiary consequences.

prompt: An officer lawfully sees an object but must enter a separately protected space to grab it. Which requirement remains unresolved?
options: Lawful access to the object.
Whether discovery was surprising.
Whether the officer can name the object’s color.
Whether the owner dislikes police.
explanation: Plain view requires lawful vantage, lawful access, and probable cause regarding incriminating character.

prompt: During a lawful emergency entry, an officer moves stereo equipment to expose serial numbers based only on reasonable suspicion. What is the strongest objection?
options: Every object may be moved whenever officers enter lawfully.
The manipulation is an additional search not justified by plain view alone.
Reasonable suspicion always satisfies the plain-view seizure standard.
The emergency authorizes unrelated evidence exploration indefinitely.
explanation: Distinguish seeing what is exposed from manipulating to reveal more.

prompt: During a lawful frisk, an officer knows a lump is not a weapon but squeezes it to identify drugs. What is the issue?
options: Every frisk authorizes a general evidence search.
Officers must ignore contraband even when immediately apparent through lawful touching.
Extra probing after the weapon concern ends exceeds the lawful frisk.
All pocket contents are unprotected once a stop begins.
explanation: Plain feel can support seizure only when incriminating character becomes apparent through lawful touching.

prompt: Officers conducting a protective sweep open a coin box too small to hold a person. What is wrong?
options: A safety sweep always includes every container.
All post-arrest searches have identical scope.
A search for people is automatically a search for documents.
A protective sweep is limited to spaces where a dangerous person could hide.
explanation: A sweep is a limited safety check of places a dangerous person could hide.

prompt: Police have probable cause only that one identified bag in a readily mobile car contains drugs. How far does that justification extend?
options: To searching that bag under the automobile exception, not automatically the entire car.
To every compartment regardless of the object-specific probable cause.
To every nearby residence.
To every occupant’s digital phone contents.
explanation: Object-specific probable cause can define a narrower search than whole-vehicle probable cause.

prompt: Officers have probable cause about a motorcycle covered inside home curtilage. Does the automobile exception alone allow entry there?
options: Yes; any motor vehicle cancels curtilage protection.
No; the vehicle exception does not itself authorize crossing protected curtilage to reach the motorcycle.
Yes; probable cause removes every location-based limit.
No; a vehicle on a public road can never be searched without a warrant.
explanation: The authority to search a vehicle does not automatically supply authority to enter protected curtilage.

prompt: Officers have probable cause directed at a bag in a car. The owner argues that every closed container in a vehicle always needs its own warrant. Which answer is best?
options: Every closed bag is categorically immune from the automobile exception.
Placing a bag in a car eliminates all limits on its search.
The automobile exception can authorize the bag search within the scope of probable cause; a separate-container warrant is not categorically required.
Probable cause is unnecessary whenever a container is portable.
explanation: A brief should distinguish the earlier holding from later doctrinal change.

prompt: A readily mobile motor home sits in a public lot and probable cause supports a contraband search. Does its possible use for sleeping automatically defeat the automobile exception?
options: Yes; any sleeping capacity always makes a vehicle a fixed home.
No; wheels alone permit a search without probable cause.
Yes; a vehicle must actually be moving when searched.
No; mobility and its vehicle-like setting can bring it within the exception.
explanation: Carney stresses mobility and vehicle-associated privacy expectations in its circumstances.

prompt: Police arrest a person in a living room and invoke search incident to arrest to search every room and drawer. What is the strongest response?
options: The basic exception reaches the arrestee and immediate control area, not the entire house.
The whole address automatically becomes part of the arrestee’s person.
The exception permits any search if requesting a warrant is inconvenient.
No search of the arrestee’s person can occur without another warrant.
explanation: Search-incident scope must remain connected to the applicable arrest doctrine.

prompt: An officer issues only a traffic citation, then searches the car solely because she could have made an arrest. Best analysis?
options: Potential arrest authority is always equivalent to an actual custodial arrest.
Unused authority to arrest does not create a search-incident exception after a citation alone.
Every traffic citation permits a full vehicle search.
A driver loses all privacy by accepting the ticket.
explanation: An available power to arrest is not the same as exercising it.

prompt: An arrested driver is secured away from the car, and the arrest offense supplies no reason to expect evidence inside. Does search incident to arrest authorize a passenger-compartment search?
options: Yes; any recent occupant’s arrest automatically permits it.
Yes; all cars contain evidence of every offense.
No on those facts; another independent justification would be needed.
No; cars are immune from every recognized search exception.
explanation: Gant requires reachability at the time or a reasonable belief of evidence of the arrest offense.

prompt: Police seize a smartphone during a lawful arrest. Can they generally browse its stored messages under search incident to arrest alone?
options: Yes; all digital data is treated exactly like an ordinary physical pocket container.
Yes; lawful seizure automatically authorizes every content search.
No phone may ever be secured as evidence.
No; a warrant is generally required for the digital contents unless an independent exception applies.
explanation: Riley distinguishes securing the device from exploring its extensive digital information.

prompt: A resident allows entry after officers assert that they have a warrant. The government later relies only on consent. What is the problem?
options: Submission to asserted legal authority does not establish voluntary consent.
Every consent search must use a notarized form.
Every spoken agreement is automatically voluntary.
An officer’s assertion creates a valid judicial warrant.
explanation: Analyze whether permission was freely given, not just whether words of agreement were spoken.

prompt: An occupant agrees to a vehicle search without being told she can refuse. Which approach best tests consent?
options: The absence of a warning automatically invalidates every consent.
Examine voluntariness under all the circumstances; lack of a refusal warning is relevant but not automatically decisive.
Saying yes conclusively establishes voluntariness despite threats.
Consent is valid only if a lawyer was present.
explanation: Knowledge of the right to refuse is relevant, but Schneckloth does not impose it as an absolute prerequisite.

prompt: One physically present co-resident expressly refuses an evidentiary home search while another consents. With no other justification, which is best?
options: A consenting co-resident always overrides a present express objection.
The objection permanently bars every later consent even after lawful removal.
The other resident’s consent does not override the present objector’s refusal as against that objector.
Officers may automatically arrest the objector solely to avoid the refusal.
explanation: Fernandez separately addresses consent after objectively lawful removal of an objector.

prompt: A person seems to share access to a home but actually lacks authority. Can apparent authority ever justify police reliance?
options: Yes, whenever the person sounds confident, regardless of contrary facts.
No reasonable factual mistake can ever be considered.
Only the property’s titled owner can ever consent.
Yes, if the belief is objectively reasonable; unresolved ambiguity may require inquiry.
explanation: Illinois v. Rodriguez focuses on objectively reasonable beliefs about common authority.

prompt: A city demands hotel guest records immediately, punishing refusal without any opportunity for precompliance review. It relies only on calling hotels closely regulated. Best analysis?
options: Hotels are not automatically in that category; the missing opportunity for neutral review creates a constitutional problem.
Every licensed business is a closely regulated industry.
Administrative purpose eliminates all safeguards.
Operating a hotel waives all Fourth Amendment protection.
explanation: Administrative inspection authority must include the required safeguards or rest on an actual exception.

prompt: A statute permits inspections in a closely regulated industry but gives inspectors unlimited discretion over time, place, and scope. What is the strongest concern?
options: The industry label alone validates unlimited discretion.
The scheme lacks an adequate substitute for a warrant’s notice and limits, even if a substantial regulatory interest exists.
Any warrantless regulatory inspection is forbidden in all circumstances.
Only the owner’s willingness to cooperate matters.
explanation: All parts of the framework matter; regulation alone does not suffice.

prompt: A routine housing inspection lacks individual suspicion of a crime. Is a warrant necessarily impossible?
options: Yes; a warrant always needs individualized criminal suspicion.
No warrant or consent is ever required for a housing inspection.
No; reasonable inspection-program standards can supply administrative probable cause.
Inspectors must first prove a code crime beyond a reasonable doubt.
explanation: Administrative probable cause differs from ordinary criminal probable cause, while preserving review safeguards.

prompt: Police inventory a lawfully impounded vehicle under standard caretaking procedures. What is the best analysis?
options: Calling it inventory automatically excuses any evidence hunt.
A missing criminal warrant automatically defeats every inventory.
Every inventory permits searches of unrelated homes.
Evaluate lawful impoundment, genuine inventory purpose, and standardized scope under the relevant doctrine.
explanation: Opperman recognizes a legitimate caretaking inventory in its circumstances, not a free-standing label that cures pretextual searches.

prompt: A search violated the Fourth Amendment. Which conclusion is premature?
options: The entire criminal case must automatically be dismissed.
The particular evidence and requested remedy need analysis.
The defendant’s own affected rights matter.
Limits on exclusion may affect admissibility.
explanation: The violation, suppression remedy, and ability to prosecute with other evidence are separate questions.

prompt: An officer relies on a warrant plainly missing its description of things to be seized and claims good faith. What is the strongest obstacle?
options: Every signed warrant guarantees good faith regardless of defects.
An obvious facial defect may make reliance objectively unreasonable.
Good faith eliminates the particularity requirement itself.
Subjective sincerity alone ends the inquiry.
explanation: Leon’s limits include facial deficiency; Groh illustrates why an obvious particularity problem matters.

prompt: At trial the prosecutor proves that the defendant probably committed the charged crime, but a reasonable doubt remains about an essential element. Is that enough to convict?
options: Yes; a fair probability is sufficient at trial.
Yes; reasonable suspicion is the highest criminal burden.
No; each offense element must be proved beyond a reasonable doubt.
Yes; an earlier arrest relieves the prosecution of proving elements.
explanation: Winship requires the high criminal burden; earlier investigation and arrest standards are lower.

prompt: Officers reasonably rely on a warrant later found unsupported by probable cause. There are no material lies, obvious defects, abandoned judicial neutrality, or bare-bones support. Must the evidence always be excluded?
options: Yes; every constitutional defect automatically requires exclusion.
No; the defect becomes constitutionally valid retroactively.
No; subjective politeness alone would cure any deliberate violation.
No; objectively reasonable reliance can limit exclusion even though the warrant was defective.
explanation: Leon concerns the exclusionary remedy and has important exceptions; it does not erase the underlying warrant defect.

prompt: An earlier unlawful search is followed by a valid warrant based on genuinely independent information, and the decision to seek it was not prompted by the illegal search. What is the best argument for admitting the later-acquired evidence?
options: The independent-source doctrine can apply if the lawful acquisition is genuinely independent.
Every later event is permanently tainted regardless of independence.
The successful illegal search retroactively became lawful.
Any second officer automatically supplies independence.
explanation: Murray asks whether the later lawful acquisition is genuinely independent of the earlier illegality.

prompt: Police unlawfully find an object, but claim a lawful ongoing investigation would inevitably have located it anyway. What must that argument establish?
options: The object existed, so discovery was inevitable.
The lawful route would inevitably have produced the evidence; mere possibility is not enough.
Any officer believes it might have been found someday.
The illegal search was efficient.
explanation: Nix recognizes inevitable discovery with proof of the lawful route, not speculation based on the search’s success.

prompt: A resident consents to a search for a missing full-size shield. Can officers rely solely on that consent to open a tiny ring box?
options: Yes; consent to any search always permits every container.
Yes; the word search has no limits.
No; objectively reasonable scope is tied to what was authorized.
No consent search can ever include containers.
explanation: Jimeno uses objective reasonableness to assess scope. The stated object limits places it could reasonably be found.

prompt: A state seeks conviction for a serious criminal offense despite one juror voting not guilty. What constitutional issue should the defense raise?
options: A right to a grand jury in every state prosecution.
An automatic right to choose the verdict personally.
A rule abolishing all state juries.
The jury-unanimity requirement for a serious criminal conviction.
explanation: Keep the underlying unanimity holding separate from the later question of which final cases receive its benefit.
